The anti-vortex film cooling concept proposes adding two branched holes from each primary hole to produce a vorticity counter to the detrimental kidney vortices.

Two main anti-vortex hole configurations were studied: the 'upstream' design with side holes emerging upstream of the main jet, and the 'adjacent' design with side holes emerging adjacent to the main jet.
The key geometric parameters were: hole diameter ratio (d/d_m = 0.5), side hole angle (105.67° for adjacent, 90° for upstream), and spanwise pitch (p/d = 3.0).
The computational study considered blowing ratios (M) of 1.0 and 2.0, and density ratios (DR) of 1.0 and 2.0.
The computational results showed the 'adjacent' anti-vortex design improved film cooling effectiveness compared to both the baseline round hole and the previous 'upstream' anti-vortex design.
A side hole diameter ratio of 0.5 was used, as a lower ratio of 0.25 was found to perform more poorly due to insufficient coolant flow through the side holes.
Unlike a staggered row of round holes, the anti-vortex design does not increase the overall coolant flow rate for a given plenum pressure.

Potential benefits of the anti-vortex design include easier manufacturability, potential for improved cooling in turbines subject to deposition, and alternate coolant flow paths if one hole becomes plugged.
Potential limitations include the lower limit on side hole diameter and the need to optimize the side hole size and angle to balance the counter-rotating vorticity generation.
The computational domain extended from the hole centerline to the mid-pitch plane, with symmetry boundary conditions applied.
The simulations were performed using the Glenn-HT CFD code with the k-ω turbulence model and a fine grid of approximately 2.5 million cells.
Convergence was achieved when residuals were reduced by 3 orders of magnitude and no observable change in surface temperature prediction occurred.
The baseline round hole case showed the characteristic kidney vortices and jet lift-off at the high blowing ratio (M=2, DR=2) condition.
The anti-vortex designs were able to mitigate the jet lift-off and improve the film cooling effectiveness compared to the baseline round hole.

The adjacent anti-vortex design required a similar plenum pressure to the baseline round hole to achieve the same blowing ratio, unlike a staggered row arrangement which would increase the overall coolant flow rate.
